```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)
```


# Problem 1

I wrote a function to simulate birthdays for a group of people and check whether at least two people share the same birthday. Each birthday is randomly sampled from 365 possible days with replacement. The function returns TRUE if there is a shared birthday and FALSE otherwise.


```{r birthday-function}
birthday_match = function(group_size) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, group_size, replace = TRUE)
  n_distinct(birthdays) < group_size
}
```

## Running the simulations

I ran the function 10,000 times for each group size from 2 to 50 and recorded whether a shared birthday occurred in each simulation.

```{r birthday-simulations}
birthday_sim_df =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iteration = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(shared_birthday = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_match))
```


## Estimating the probabilities

For each group size, I estimated the probability of a shared birthday by taking the mean of the simulation results. Since TRUE is treated as 1 and FALSE as 0, the mean gives the proportion of simulations with a shared birthday.

```{r birthday-summary}
birthday_prob_df = 
  birthday_sim_df |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(probability = mean(shared_birthday))

birthday_prob_df |>
  filter(group_size %in% c(2, 10, 23, 30, 40, 50)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Plotting the probabilities

The following plot shows how the estimated probability of a shared birthday changes with group size.

```{r birthday-plot}
birthday_prob_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a Shared Birthday by Group Size",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Estimated probability"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1), limits = c(0, 1))
```

## Results

The estimated probability of a shared birthday increases as the group size grows. For a group of 23 people, the estimated probability is `r round(100 * birthday_prob_df$probability[birthday_prob_df$group_size == 23], 1)`%, while for a group of 50 people, it increases to `r round(100 * birthday_prob_df$probability[birthday_prob_df$group_size == 50], 1)`%. The probability reaches approximately 50% with only 23 people, which is surprising given that there are 365 possible birthdays.


# Problem 2

## Importing the data

I first listed all the participant files and used `map()` to read each file into a list column.

```{r import, message=FALSE}
participant_files_df =
  tibble(file_name = list.files("./data", pattern = "^con_|^exp_")) |>
  mutate(
    subject_data = purrr::map(
      file_name,
      \(file) read_csv(str_c("./data/", file))
    )
  )
```


## Tidying the data

I used the file names to get the study arm and subject ID. Then I combined the files and reshaped the weekly measurements so that each row represents one subject in one week.

```{r tidy}
study_tidy_df =
  participant_files_df |>
  separate(
    file_name,
    into = c("arm", "subject_id"),
    sep = "_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arm = str_replace(arm, "con", "Control"),
    arm = str_replace(arm, "exp", "Experimental"),
    subject_id = str_replace(subject_id, "\\.csv$", "")
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = "subject_data") |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(str_replace(week, "week_", ""))
  ) |>
  select(arm, subject_id, week, observation) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

study_tidy_df |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(
    n_subjects = n_distinct(subject_id),
    n_observations = n()
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```


## Spaghetti plot

I plotted each subject's measurements over the eight weeks and separated the two study arms to compare their patterns.

```{r plot}
study_tidy_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = subject_id,
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = .7) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly Observations by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Results

The experimental group generally shows an upward trend over time, although the rate of increase varies between subjects. Most experimental subjects start between about -1 and 4 in week 1 and end between about 3 and 7 in week 8. In contrast, the control group stays relatively stable, mostly between about -1 and 3, with some week-to-week fluctuations but no clear trend.

The two groups start at fairly similar levels in week 1, but the gap gets larger over time. By week 8, all subjects in the experimental group have higher observations than the subjects in the control group.



# Problem 3

## Simulation

I simulated 5,000 datasets for each true mean from 0 to 6, using a sample size of 30 and a standard deviation of 5. For each dataset, I ran a one-sample t-test and saved the estimated mean and p-value.

```{r}
sim_ttest = function(true_mu) {
  sim_data = rnorm(30, mean = true_mu, sd = 5)
  t.test(sim_data, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(1)

sim_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iteration = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_result = map(true_mu, sim_ttest)
  ) |>
  unnest(test_result) |>
  mutate(
    reject_null = p.value < 0.05
  )
```


## Statistical power

I calculated the proportion of tests that rejected the null hypothesis for each true mean, using a significance level of 0.05.

```{r power}
power_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject_null)
  )

power_df |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r power-plot}
power_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejecting H0"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, .25, .5, .75, 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  )
```

Power increases as the effect size (the true mean) increases. When the true mean is 0, the null hypothesis is actually true, so the rejection rate of `r round(power_df$power[power_df$true_mu == 0], 3)` is the type I error rate, and it is close to 0.05 as expected. Power is low when the true mean is 1 (`r round(power_df$power[power_df$true_mu == 1], 3)`), increases quickly between 1 and 3, and is close to 1 once the true mean is 4 or larger. With the same sample size and standard deviation, larger effects are much easier to detect.


## Average estimated mean

I first calculated the average estimated mean across all 5,000 simulations for each true mean. I then calculated the average again using only the tests that rejected the null hypothesis.

```{r estimates}
mean_estimates_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate)
  )

rejected_estimates_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  filter(reject_null) |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate_rejected = mean(estimate)
  )

mean_comparison_df =
  mean_estimates_df |>
  left_join(rejected_estimates_df, by = "true_mu") |>
  mutate(
    true_mean = true_mu
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    mean_estimate:true_mean,
    names_to = "estimate_type",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    estimate_type = str_replace(
      estimate_type, "mean_estimate_rejected", "Rejected tests"
    ),
    estimate_type = str_replace(
      estimate_type, "mean_estimate", "All tests"
    ),
    estimate_type = str_replace(
      estimate_type, "true_mean", "True mean"
    )
  )
```

## Comparing the estimates

The following plot compares the average estimated means from all tests and rejected tests with the true mean.

```{r estimates-plot}
mean_comparison_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = true_mu,
      y = average_estimate,
      color = estimate_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean by True Mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = "Estimate type"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6)
```


## Results

Across all 5,000 simulations, the average estimated mean is very close to the true mean for every value of the true mean, as expected.

However, the average estimate among tests that rejected the null is not approximately equal to the true mean when the true mean is small. For example, when the true mean is 1, the average estimate among rejected tests is `r round(rejected_estimates_df$mean_estimate_rejected[rejected_estimates_df$true_mu == 1], 2)`, which is much larger than 1. This is because we only keep the samples where the test was significant. With a sample size of 30 and a standard deviation of 5, the estimate needs to be roughly 1.9 or more away from 0 for the test to reject, so when power is low, the rejected samples are mostly the ones with unusually large estimates.

As the true mean increases, power gets close to 1, so almost all tests reject the null and the average estimate among rejected tests becomes close to the true mean (for true means of 4, 5, and 6 they are nearly the same). At a true mean of zero, significant estimates fall on both sides of zero and roughly cancel out, so their average is still close to zero.
